reason: The quote says that to reference a security group in another AWS account but the same Region, you include the account number with the security group ID, for a peer VPC.

The quote supports referencing peer security groups in inbound or outbound rules, but the claim is stated generally while the page's Requirements list limits it: the peering connection must be active and a peer VPC in a different Region cannot be referenced (use its CIDR); these conditions stand only in the surrounding text.
The quote says only VPC owners can describe, create, accept, reject, modify or delete peering connections and participants cannot; owner and participant are the shared-VPC roles.
Under the heading VPC sharing, the quote lists lower costs with no data transfer charges between instances of different accounts within the same Availability Zone.
The quote states the owner shares one or more subnets with participants, who can view, create, modify and delete their own resources but not those of other participants or the owner.

The quote states subnet sharing uses implicit routing within a VPC for highly interconnected applications in the same trust boundary and reduces the number of VPCs, with separate accounts for billing and access control.
The claim restates the quote: sharing VPCs is useful when network isolation need not be strictly managed by the owner but account-level users and permissions must be.
The quote states route tables use longest prefix match to select the most specific route across the intended peering connection and all other traffic takes the next matching route.
The quote states that in these examples a central VPC is peered to at least two VPCs with overlapping CIDR blocks; the claim keeps the reference to the guide's examples.
The quote states the owner of the accepter VPC accepts the request to activate the peering connection.
The quote states the requester owner sends the request, the accepter can be owned by another account, and its CIDR cannot overlap the requester's.

The quote supports that each owner must manually add a route to the peer VPC's range to enable traffic over private IPs, but the timing clause 'after a peering connection is active' comes only from the step order in the surrounding text, and the claim drops the quote's purpose condition (to enable traffic using private IP addresses).
The quote states that, if required, you update the instance security group rules so peer traffic is not restricted, and in the same Region you can reference a peer security group.
The quote states tags created for a peering connection are only applied in the account or Region where you create them.
The quote supports only the Reachability Analyzer part; the network ACL check of the subnets stands in a separate bullet of the surrounding text, not in the quote.
Under the troubleshooting heading, the quote says to verify that each resource's subnet route table has a route sending peer-VPC traffic to the peering connection.
Under the troubleshooting heading, the quote says to verify that the instances' security groups allow inbound and outbound traffic from the peer VPC.
The REL02-BP05 quote states VPC IP ranges must not overlap when peered, connected via Transit Gateway, or connected over VPN.
The quote recommends an IPAM such as Amazon VPC IP Address Manager to monitor and manage CIDR use, under the best practice heading on non-overlapping ranges.
The quote supports the whitepaper's maximum of 125 active peering connections per VPC, but the qualifier condition (quotas page default of 50, raisable to 125) is not in the quote.
The quote states peering is best when resources must communicate, both environments are controlled and secured, and fewer than 10 VPCs are connected for individual management.
The quote states transfer within an AZ is free, cross-AZ is charged at standard in-region rates, and inter-Region peering pays standard inter-Region charges.
The two quotes state peering enables full bidirectional connectivity between the VPCs and is point-to-point without transitive routing.
The quote states a full mesh of 100 VPCs takes 4,950 peering connections by n(n-1)/2; 100x99/2 = 4,950.
The quote states peering offers the lowest overall cost and highest aggregate performance compared to other inter-VPC options.
The quote contrasts many-to-many (traffic managed individually per VPC pair) with hub-and-spoke (all traffic through a central resource routing by rules).
The quote states on-premises connectivity must be made to each VPC with peering, since a VPC cannot use a peered VPC's hybrid connectivity.
The quote states VPC-to-VPC connectivity is best with non-overlapping ranges and advises a single, contiguous, non-overlapping CIDR block per VPC.
The quote states full connectivity with peering needs 1:1 connections between each VPC pair, or alternatively Transit Gateway or Cloud WAN as a transit hub.
